lessons.title: You are the security team
lessons.content:
# You are the security team

A bank has fraud analysts, a frozen-card button, and a number a human answers. Self-custody gives you **finality** — a completed send is not a customer-care undo. It also gives you **the job**.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say, in your own words, what a threat model is, which security model you are in for each pile of value you hold, and why “I am careful” is not a defence unless it is a checklist.

## Finality is the feature that also fires the security team

**Finality** means: after a payment has settled under the system’s rules, there is no help desk that reverses it because you are sorry. You already met this idea in Foundations. It is the reason crypto can settle a gift across a border on a Sunday. It is also the reason the same rails will settle a theft with the same calm.

A card network often has a **chargeback**: a customer disputes a payment and the scheme may reverse it. That parenting is expensive. It is why merchants get frozen, why KYC exists, and why a stolen debit card is sometimes a phone call instead of a funeral. Public chains mostly do not parent you. The book is public. The signature was valid. The transfer is done.

This is not a sermon against self-custody. It is the job description. If you hold keys, you are the security team. If you hold an exchange IOU, you share the job with a company — and you can still fail your half by handing them a phished login.

## Three security models, named so you stop mixing them

People lose funds because they describe the wrong model. They say “the blockchain will freeze it” about an exchange IOU, or “I’ll call support” about an on-chain send.

**1. Bank / card model.** You plus an institution’s security team. Reversal is sometimes possible. Identity checks are the price. A freeze can save you and can also lock you out.

**2. Centralised exchange model.** You plus the company’s security team. The number on the screen is an **IOU** — a row in their ledger, not coins at an address you control. They may freeze a withdrawal. They may recover an account if you still pass their identity checks. They will not reverse an on-chain withdrawal that already left. Binance, here and in the rest of this course, is **an example of a centralised exchange**, not “the only real one.”

**3. Self-custody model.** You. The coins sit on the chain at an address whose **private key** you control. A **private key** is the secret that can sign. A **seed phrase** is the human backup of that secret (usually 12 or 24 words). There is no parent. There is also no password reset.

TABLE
Model | Who is on the security team | What a parent can still do | What a parent cannot do
Bank / card | You + the institution | Freeze, reverse some payments, replace a card | Invent cash you already handed to a stranger
Centralised exchange | You + the company | Kill sessions, reset a login, sometimes freeze an IOU | Reverse a completed on-chain withdrawal; invent a seed you leaked
Self-custody | You | Nothing at the protocol layer | The chain will not “refund” a valid signature
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Amaka keeps 40 USDT on an exchange she bookmarked, 15 USDT in a software wallet she uses to practise, and her salary in a bank. On Monday a Telegram “support agent” wants her seed “to unsuspend Crystal Stones.” On Tuesday a Google ad wants her exchange password. On Wednesday her debit card is cloned.

1. She names the model for each pile before she answers anyone.
2. The seed request is self-custody. There is no support agent. She refuses. The 15 USDT stays.
3. The Google ad is the exchange model. She ignores the ad, opens her bookmark, and does not type a password into a search result. The 40 USDT IOU stays.
4. The cloned card is the bank model. She calls the number on the back of the *physical* card, not a number in an SMS. The bank may reverse some charges.

Three piles. Three models. One person who stopped treating “careful” as a personality.

DIAGRAM
Bank model:       you + institution's fraud team
Exchange model:   you + company's security team
                  (you can still get phished)
Self-custody:     you
                  (the chain will settle a theft as calmly as a gift)

Name the model before you answer a message.
ENDDIAGRAM

## What “threat model” means in this academy

A **threat model** is an honest list: what you have, who might want it, which attacks are actually likely, and what you will refuse even when your hands shake.

Yours, as a Crystal Stones Academy beginner, is not “a nation-state implant in the CPU.” That sentence is how people skip the boring work. The likely list is ordinary:

- phishing sites and fake apps
- impersonation in Telegram, WhatsApp, SMS, and X
- P2P receipt fraud (you already saw this in the exchanges course)
- unlimited **approvals** on clone dApps — an approval is on-chain permission for a spender to pull tokens later
- friends, cousins, and “helpers” who should not hold keys
- your own panic, which is a tool attackers manufacture on purpose

Ordinary is what empties wallets. Movie hackers are a distraction. If your threat model is “I am not important enough to hack,” you have already lost the plot. Attackers do not need you to be important. They need you to be hurried.

## “I am careful” is not a control

Careful is a story people tell after they pasted a seed into a Google Doc “backup,” used SMS as their only 2FA, and connected a wallet to three airdrop sites this week. **2FA** means **two-factor authentication**: a second proof besides the password, such as an authenticator app code. SMS 2FA is a weak second factor because a **SIM-swap** (someone convincing your mobile operator to move your number) can steal the texts.

Careful, in this course, is a checklist you can run when you are tired. Module 6 will hand you a weekly one. Today you only need the posture: identity is not security. Habits are.

NOTE
This course will repeat uncomfortable sentences. Repetition is the point. A one-time warning is how people nod and then sign a permit. Crystal Stones Academy will never ask for a seed phrase, a private key, a 2FA code, or remote control of your screen. If a message claims otherwise, it is not us — even if it has our crystal.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

You are not here to become a professional security engineer. You are here so that “who is the security team for this pile?” is a reflex, and so that finality stops being a slogan and starts being a reason to practise small.

## Say this out loud

- Self-custody means I am the security team. The chain will not parent me.
- An exchange balance is an IOU. The company is a parent for that IOU, not for a withdrawal that already left.
- A threat model is a list of likely attacks, not a feeling that I am careful.
- Likely attacks are phishing, impersonation, P2P fraud, and approvals — not movie hackers.
- “I am careful” needs a checklist I can run when I am tired.

Next: what attackers actually want from you — seed, session, approval, OTP, and the panic that opens all of them.

lessons.title: What attackers actually want (seed, session, approval, OTP, human panic)
lessons.content:
# What attackers actually want (seed, session, approval, OTP, human panic)

They do not want to “hack the blockchain.” They want **authority you already have**. Cryptography is doing its job. The book will record whatever valid signature you (or malware on your phone) produce. The attacker’s craft is getting you to produce it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to look at a message, a popup, or a phone call and name the loot: seed, session, approval, OTP, a mistaken send, a mule slot, or your audience. Naming the loot is how you pick the refuse-line before your hands shake.

## Ranked loot, from worst to merely expensive

**1. Seed phrase or private key.** Total, durable control of that wallet, on every network that seed derives, including deposits you have not made yet. There is no “change password” on a seed. Rotation — a new wallet, a test send, a move, retirement of the old words — is the only honest response. Module 5 is that procedure. Today: treat a seed request as a robbery in progress, not a support ticket.

**2. Exchange session.** Password plus **OTP** (one-time password — the 2FA code), or a stolen cookie that keeps you “logged in.” This loot spends the IOU. It does not spend on-chain coins at an address you still control, unless they also withdraw to themselves and your whitelist is off. A **withdrawal whitelist** is a company setting: withdrawals may only go to addresses you already approved, often with a delay when you add a new one.

**3. Unlimited token approval.** They pull USDT (or Crystal Stones, or whatever you approved) later. You still have the seed. You have a mystery of “I didn’t send.” You did not. You loaded a gun last month. Module 4 is this door in slow motion.

**4. One honest send to the wrong address.** Paste attack, fake invoice, QR that does not match its caption, wrong network. The signature is yours. The destination is theirs. A test send is the cheap version of this lesson.

**5. You as a mule.** They want your KYC-facing account to move stolen funds. **KYC** is Know Your Customer: the identity file an exchange or bank holds. If you “receive USDT and forward it, keep a cut,” you may be washing someone else’s theft through your name.

**6. Your audience.** Hijack your Telegram, WhatsApp, or X. The next ten people trust your face. The loot is not your 20 USDT. It is theirs.

Different loot, different popups. If you know which loot a message is aiming at, you do not need a whitepaper to refuse.

TABLE
What they say | Loot they want | Door they are opening
“Import seed to sync / migrate / restore support” | Keys | Device
“Send the 2FA code to verify this is you” | Exchange or email session | Account
“Approve to claim / verify / mint” | Allowance | Chain permission
“Sign to confirm you are human” (unread hex) | Often allowance in a costume | Chain permission
“Send 1 USDT to validate the wallet” | Direct transfer | Human, then a send
“Receive this USDT and forward it” | Mule slot | Human + your KYC
“Make me admin / drop the APK in the group” | Audience, then everyone else’s keys | Human
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Jordan sees “Official Crystal Stones airdrop — connect and sign to claim.” He has memorised “never type 12 words.” He feels safe. He connects. The wallet shows a signature, not a seed box. He signs.

1. Name the loot. This was not Door 1. This was an approval or a **permit** (a signature that grants a spender the same right as an on-chain approve, without the approve transaction). Loot type 3.
2. He still has his seed. That is not comfort. USDT can leave tonight or in August.
3. The refuse-line he needed was not “I don’t type words.” It was “I don’t sign what I cannot read, on a site I did not bookmark.”
4. He later opens a bookmarked explorer, finds the spender, and revokes from a tool he saved on a calm day — not from the airdrop site’s “disconnect” button.

The student who only memorised seed-safety is the student this course is for.

## Human panic is a loot type of its own

Attackers manufacture **cortisol**: the body chemistry of hurry. A timer on a banner. “Your funds will be lost in 10 minutes.” “AML freeze, pay to unlock.” “Last train for the snapshot.” Panic is not a side effect. Panic is the product, because panic makes you skip the bookmark, skip the middle characters of an address, and skip the sentence “what loot is this?”

You cannot out-argue a timer with more speed. You out-argue it by treating every timer as a **prop**. Chains do not confiscate for ignoring a banner. Exchanges do not unsuspend accounts via a Telegram OTP. This academy does not run a 10-minute confiscation window.

A useful private sentence, said before you tap: **“If this were real, it would still be real in twenty minutes, and I would start from a bookmark.”** If the offer dies in twenty minutes, it was never an offer.

DIAGRAM
Attacker
  |
  +--> seed / private key     (owns the wallet from now on)
  +--> session + OTP          (owns the exchange IOU for a while)
  +--> approval / permit      (owns a loaded gun against your tokens)
  +--> one wrong send         (owns that payment)
  +--> you as mule            (owns your KYC as a pipe)
  +--> your group             (owns the next ten people)
  +--> your panic             (opens every line above)

They do not need to "break BscScan."
ENDDIAGRAM

## OTP is not a conversation

An **OTP** is a one-time code. Authenticator apps generate them. SMS delivers them. Email sometimes delivers them. The code proves that the person at the keyboard can see a second device or inbox. It is not a greeting. It is not “verification” you send to a helper. Anyone who asks you to read an OTP aloud is asking for your session.

Same rule for **backup codes** — the paper codes an exchange gives you when you turn on 2FA. They are spare keys. They are not customer-care trivia.

NOTE
Nobody needs to defeat cryptography if you will hand them the key, the session, the allowance, or the OTP. The chain, and the exchange database, will then honestly help them. That honesty is not a bug. It is why settlement works when you meant the payment too.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

So that the next time a screen asks you for something, you name the loot in one word before you type. Seed. Session. Approval. OTP. Send. Mule. Audience. Panic. If you cannot name it, you reject.

## Say this out loud

- Attackers want authority I already have. They do not need to break the chain.
- Seed is the worst leak. It is not the only leak.
- Approve-to-claim and “sign to verify” can be loot even when no 12 words appear.
- An OTP is a session key. I do not read it to a helper.
- Panic is manufactured. If it would still be real in twenty minutes, I start from a bookmark.

Next: the four doors as a map — device, account, chain permission, and human — so every later scam has a name.

lessons.title: The four doors (device, account, chain permission, human)
lessons.content:
# The four doors (device, account, chain permission, human)

Memorise four. Every scam in later modules is one of these, sometimes two stacked. Naming the door is not wordplay. It tells you the fix. People who only say “I was hacked” cannot pick a fix, so they pick a recovery wizard.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to point at a bad afternoon and say which door opened, which loot left, and which door is still shut.

## Door 1 — Device (the keys live here)

The **device** is the phone, laptop, browser profile, or hardware box where signing happens. Attackers who win this door get the seed, the private key, or malware that can sign as you.

Typical openings:

- a cloned wallet app, or an APK (Android package file) from a chat
- a seed typed into a website “to sync”
- a screenshot of the words in a gallery or a cloud notes app
- overlay malware that draws a fake window on a real app
- a hardware device whose screen you ignored while the laptop lied

If they have the words, they have the wallet on every EVM chain that seed derives, including future deposits. **Rotation** (new seed on a clean device, test, move, retire old) is the only honest response. There is no “change password” on a seed. Module 5 will walk that procedure without asking you to send leftovers to a specialist.

Hardware wallets help **if you read the device screen**. They do not help if you tap confirm because the phone looked familiar. “I have a hardware wallet, so I can sign anything blindly” is a quiz answer this course will fail on purpose.

## Door 2 — Account (the company still has a parent)

**Account** means exchange login, email, Apple or Google store account, academy login, the SIM that receives SMS. This door has a parent — the company — and also has phishing.

Typical openings:

- a fake login page from an ad
- a SIM-swap against SMS 2FA
- password reuse from a leaked site
- an OTP read to a “support agent”
- a session cookie on a shared or stolen laptop

The fix is the parent’s security page: kill sessions, rotate password, rotate 2FA, check the withdrawal whitelist. The fix is never a Telegram handle that arrived after you tweeted “withdrawal stuck.”

Academy login is Door 2 for **this site** (progress, not your BNB). Still: do not reuse the exchange password on the academy. Password reuse is how one leak becomes three doors.

## Door 3 — Chain permission (the gun you loaded)

**Chain permission** is an on-chain or off-chain signature that lets someone else move tokens without holding your seed. The common names: **approval**, **allowance**, **permit**, **setApprovalForAll** for NFTs.

You still hold the seed. The spender is loaded. Days later, `transferFrom` can run while you sleep. Your wallet may not pop up. BscScan will show the spender. People say “I didn’t click Send.” Correct. They clicked Approve last month.

**Revoke** — a new transaction that sets that spender’s allowance to zero — is the response when the seed is still yours. If the seed may also be leaked, revoke on the old wallet is theatre. Rotate. Module 4 is this door in detail.

## Door 4 — Human (they change what you believe)

They change the **story**: who you are talking to, what the invoice is, whether the academy asked, whether the network is BEP-20, whether a lover is also your broker. P2P receipt fraud, romance, jobs, fake support, giveaways. No transaction is required until the last step. This is the door that opens the other three.

Typical openings:

- a display name that looks like a founder
- a “Crystal Mentor” DM
- a the checkout processor invoice pasted in WhatsApp
- a QR caption that does not match its bytes
- a timer that says you will miss the last train

The fix is not a better argument with the stranger. The fix is: stop talking, verify on a bookmark you already had, do not “finish the process.”

TABLE
Door | What they get | Typical fix if already open | What does not fix it
Device | Seed, signing malware | New wallet on a clean device; never reuse leaked words | “I changed the app PIN”
Account | Login, OTP, session | Official security page: sessions, password, 2FA, whitelist | A DM from a badge
Chain permission | Spender can pull tokens | Revoke on a known checker, then move if the device is dirty | The fake site’s Disconnect button
Human | A story you believe | Stop; bookmark; do not finish | Winning the argument
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Fatima fails Door 4: she believes a fake admin in a Crystal Stones fan group. The admin drops a “verification dApp.” She opens Door 3: she approves unlimited USDT. She never typed a seed. Post-mortem in the group says “I was hacked.”

1. Precise version: social then allowance. Door 4 opened Door 3.
2. Door 1 may still be shut — unless she typed words, installed an APK, or the phone was already dirty.
3. Door 2 is untouched. The exchange IOU is still a separate pile.
4. The fix is: reject further popups, check approvals from a bookmarked tool, revoke, consider moving remaining funds to a fresh hot wallet if the phone is a playground. Not: pay a recovery specialist in the same group. That specialist watched the group for this moment.

Precision is how you prevent the next one. “Hacked” is a fog. Fog is how the second predator works.

DIAGRAM
Door 1  DEVICE ............ seed, APK, malware, ignored hardware screen
Door 2  ACCOUNT ........... login, email, SIM, OTP, session cookie
Door 3  CHAIN PERMISSION .. approve, permit, setApprovalForAll
Door 4  HUMAN ............. the story that opens 1, 2, and 3

Most "hacks" are Door 4, then one of the others.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy never-ask-seed is Door 1 policy. We also will not ask for 2FA codes (Door 2), unlimited approves (Door 3), remote control of your screen (Door 1 + 2), or off-platform “verification payments” including “send USDT to verify” (Door 4). If a human’s request needs any of those, they are not us — even with a similar avatar.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

So that every later module has a map. Phishing is usually Door 4 opening 1, 2, or 3. People scams are Door 4 with patience. Drains are Door 3, sometimes Door 1. Incident response is: name the door, then pick the fix that matches.

## Say this out loud

- Four doors: device, account, chain permission, human.
- Naming the door tells me the fix. “Hacked” does not.
- Human is the door that opens the other three.
- A hardware wallet is still Door 1 if I confirm blindly, and still Door 3 if I approve a drainer.
- Academy staff will not ask me to open any of the four doors.

Next: practice amounts and play-money rules — the architecture that makes a mistake survivable.

lessons.title: Practice amounts and play-money rules
lessons.content:
# Practice amounts and play-money rules

Skill is built with **money you can lose**. If the amount would change rent, food, school fees, or the invoice you are waiting on, it is not a practice amount. Pride is how people practise with a month of work.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to define a practice amount in your own life, split a hot play pocket from a colder savings pocket, and refuse the sentence “I’ll make it back tonight.”

## A practice amount is a household number, not a Telegram number

A **practice amount** is a sum whose disappearance would sting your pride and not your calendar. For one student that is 3 USDT. For another, 15. For someone sending local currency through P2P, it might be the smallest the counterparty will honour. The number is local. The rule is not: **if losing it would cancel a bill, it is not practice.**

This academy will keep saying **practice with amounts you can lose** until it is boring. Boring is the point. The first send on a new network, the first token add, the first dApp, the first P2P, the first withdrawal whitelist change — all of those are practice events. They use practice size.

“Everyone in the group uses 500 USDT” is not a definition. Groups contain people who can lose 500 USDT and people who are about to be wrecked. You are not a group. You are a rent cycle.

## Five rules that sound childish and save careers

1. First week on a new wallet: only play money. Live with the app. Receive a tiny test. Send a tiny test. Confirm the explorer. Then, maybe, more.
2. First transaction on a new dApp: play money. A **dApp** is a website that asks your wallet to sign. New URL, new risk, even if the logo is familiar.
3. First time you add a custom token: verify the contract on a bookmarked explorer, still play money if you will swap. Crystal Stones, as the project publishes it, is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BNB Smart Chain. That is a **reference to verify**, not a buy order, and not a reason to skip the test send.
4. Never “make it back” the same night you lost a practice amount on a clone. Revenge-sizing is how practice becomes a hole.
5. Hardware later, for amounts that would hurt — still with a test send. A hardware box does not make a 2,000 USDT first-try a good idea.

## Two pockets is architecture, not a personality

A daily-driver software wallet should be a **spending** pocket. A second wallet (eventually hardware, at first just a second software seed you almost never connect) is the **savings** pocket. Approvals live on the spending pocket. If the spending pocket dies, the savings pocket did not sign the clone.

Moving between them is a normal on-chain send, with BNB for gas, with a test. **BNB** is the native coin on BNB Smart Chain; tokens need it for fees. Do not keep “just enough BNB to escape” only on the savings pocket if you have never practised the escape.

Two pockets means two backups. Do not invent a second seed and then screenshot both into the same Drive folder. That is one pocket wearing two hats. A cloud folder is Door 1 with extra steps.

TABLE
Pocket | What it is for | What it may connect to | What a failure should cost
Play / hot | Learning, tiny swaps, first dApps | New sites, after a bookmark check | A practice amount
Savings / colder | Rare sends, longer holds | Almost nothing; known destinations | Would hurt — so it does not visit sponsored links
Exchange IOU | On purpose, as a company balance | The bookmarked exchange app only | Whatever the company and your 2FA can still protect
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Chidi keeps everything in the same MetaMask (an **example of a wallet app**, not an endorsement) he uses to “test airdrops.” An airdrop site takes the USDT **and** the Crystal Stones **and** the BNB. There was no second pocket.

1. He named himself careful. He had one door, loaded, on every asset.
2. Architecture would have been: play pocket with 8 USDT and a little BNB; savings pocket that has never seen a sponsored link; exchange IOU separate.
3. The airdrop could still kill the play pocket. That is what play pockets are for.
4. The savings pocket would have been a boring send away, after a test, on a calm day — not during the incident.

The lesson is architecture, not luck. Luck is not a threat model.

DIAGRAM
Play pocket (hot)
   |  tiny tests, dApps you are learning
   |  approvals live here
   v
   --small sends-->  Savings pocket (colder)
                     rare connects
                     known destinations
                     hardware later, still with a test

Exchange IOU sits to the side: company ledger, 2FA, whitelist.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Panic-sizing and “dust”

**Dust** is a leftover too small to care about — a few cents of a token, a fragment of BNB. After a scare, thieves and “recovery specialists” will ask you to send the dust “so they can trace” or “so they can unlock the rest.” Do not. Dust is not a tracing fee. Dust is bait. If you rotate a leaked seed, you may leave dust behind on purpose. That is cheaper than handing a stranger a last payment.

Also: do not sweep every mystery token along when you rotate. Mystery tokens are how Door 3 gets a second chance. Hide them. Move what you already understood. Module 4 and Module 5 will say this again.

NOTE
Two pockets is not a command to buy a hardware wallet this week, and it is not a command to hold Crystal Stones. It is a command to stop storing experiments and savings behind the same signature. If you only have play money, you only need a play pocket — and you still practise small.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

So that a mistake is tuition, not a hole in the month. Safety that only works when the number is tiny is still safety. Safety that you plan to “turn on later, when it matters” is how later arrives already empty.

## Say this out loud

- A practice amount is defined by rent and food, not by a group chat.
- Hot pocket experiments. Colder pocket rarely connects.
- I do not chase a loss the same night, and I do not send leftover dust to a specialist.
- Two seeds in one cloud folder are one seed.
- Hardware does not make a large first-try safe. A test send still goes first.

Next: the academy never-ask-seed policy, written so you can quote it at a fake admin — including staff, “wallet support,” and a “token listing team.”

lessons.title: Never-ask-seed, in writing (including academy staff, wallet support, token listing team)
lessons.content:
# Never-ask-seed, in writing (including academy staff, wallet support, token listing team)

Quote this to anyone, including someone with a Crystal Stones logo, a Binance-coloured badge, a “Trust Wallet support” handle, or a business card that says token listing.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to recite what this academy will never ask for, what it may ask for, and which three costumes — staff, wallet support, listing team — use the same script.

## The policy, as a paragraph you can paste

**Crystal Stones Academy staff, mentors, and support will never ask for:**

- a seed phrase (12, 18, or 24 words)
- a private key, a keystore file, or a “secret recovery phrase”
- a wallet PIN that is actually the seed, or a screenshot of either
- a 2FA code, SMS code, email code, authenticator QR, or backup codes
- remote desktop control of your phone or laptop (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, “just share the screen”)
- a payment to a personal wallet to “unlock” a course, a certificate, a listing, a recovery, or a migration
- “verify by sending USDT” (or BNB, or Crystal Stones) to an address in a DM

**They may ask you to:**

- log into the academy site **you bookmarked**
- pay Intermediate or Advanced tuition through the **published checkout** when that track is live — USDT on BEP-20 via the published academy checkout, not Crystal Stones token, not PaynovaX, not a wallet in a DM
- paste a **transaction hash** (a public explorer id) if you are stuck
- describe what a popup said, without photographing a seed

If a human’s request is not on the second list and is on the first, they are not us — even if they have a similar avatar, even if they say they are “Mentor Grok,” even if they say they are from the listing team.

A **transaction hash** is safe to share because it is already public. It cannot, by itself, authorise spending. A seed is the opposite object.

## Costume 1 — academy staff and “Crystal Mentor”

The real Mentor, in this product, is a chat **inside** the academy app. It does not import wallets. It does not DM you first on WhatsApp. It does not need a seed to “sync Crystal Mentor AI.” A person who starts in Telegram with a crystal avatar is running Door 4.

Staff should be willing to say: “I will not finish this in WhatsApp. Open the bookmarked site.” If “staff” refuses to leave WhatsApp, they are not staff. That sentence is a test. Use it.

Certificates in Basic are **platform** certificates after quizzes, not a wallet signature. “Download certificate, sign in with wallet” is a drain costume.

## Costume 2 — “wallet support” (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, hardware brands)

Wallet companies do not restore your funds with your seed. The seed **is** the restoration. Anyone who needs the words “to help” is asking you to hand them the vault. Trust Wallet and MetaMask are **examples of wallet apps**, not endorsements, and not people who will DM you after you tweet a screenshot.

There is no “BSC migration” that requires re-entering a seed into a website. There is no “new Trust Wallet APK” that must arrive as a WhatsApp file. Official updates come from the store listing you already used on a calm day, or from the hardware maker’s own site, bookmarked.

## Costume 3 — “token listing team” and “the checkout processor billing”

Listing teams at real exchanges do not collect seeds. They do not ask retail students to “verify holdings” by sending tokens to a personal address. If you ever actually list anything, that is a company process with published forms — not a Telegram invoice.

**the checkout processor** is the checkout rail this academy has said it will use for paid tracks: USDT on BEP-20. A fake the checkout processor page is a phishing surface. Real checkout starts on the **bookmarked academy site**, not from a PDF in email, not from a WhatsApp invoice that “expires in 15 minutes.” If you did not click Checkout inside the official app, you do not owe that invoice.

The Crystal Stones contract to **verify only** is:

`0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`

A listing-team costume that sends a *different* contract “because of a migration” is a clone. Verify on bookmarked BscScan. This paragraph is still not a buy order.

TABLE
Request | Us? | Them?
“Paste 12 words to reset progress / sync Mentor” | No | Thief
“Send 0.1 BNB to verify the certificate” | No | Thief
“Open the official checkout URL from the site you bookmarked” | Yes, when you actually owe tuition | —
“What’s the tx hash on BscScan?” | Yes | Fine
“Share screen so I can fix nonce” | No | Thief
“New contract for the listing, last train” | No | Clone
“the checkout processor invoice, pay this 0x from WhatsApp” | No | Fake billing
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A WhatsApp account named “Mentor Grok” writes to Sam after she posted a quiz score in a fan group. It asks for a seed to “sync Crystal Mentor AI” and, if she hesitates, for 20 USDT “to a the checkout processor wallet so the certificate can mint.”

1. She quotes the policy. Seed is on the never-list. Personal USDT is on the never-list.
2. She does not argue about tone. Argument is how Door 4 stays open.
3. She opens the bookmarked academy app. Mentor is there. It does not know about WhatsApp.
4. She reports the number to people she already trusts **offline** if that is useful, and she does not paste her remaining address into the group as a bounty.

The refusal was the whole skill. Politeness is optional. The door staying shut is not.

DIAGRAM
Official paths
  bookmarked academy site
  in-app Mentor
  published checkout (USDT BEP-20 / the checkout processor when live)
  public tx hash

Unofficial paths
  DMs, new wallets, seeds, 2FA codes
  remote control, APKs in chat
  WhatsApp the checkout processor invoices
  "listing team" personal 0x

When in doubt, the unofficial path is a no.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
This policy also protects staff. If someone claiming to be you asks a mentor to “hold these words,” staff must refuse too. A screenshot of a seed in a gallery is not “encrypted.” It is a photograph of the vault combination, sitting next to your selfies, often backed up to a company cloud. Treat it as a leak. Rotate. Do not debate file encryption with a thief.
ENDNOTE

## What this lesson is for

So you have a paragraph, not a vibe. When a costume arrives, you do not need to research the person. You compare the ask to the two lists. First list: no. Second list: maybe, from a bookmark.

## Say this out loud

- Crystal Stones Academy never asks for seeds, private keys, 2FA, remote desktop, or “verify by sending USDT.”
- Hashes are OK. Words are not.
- Checkout is published on the bookmarked site, not pasted in WhatsApp.
- Wallet support that needs the seed to help is not support. A listing team that needs a personal send is not a listing team.
- Logo plus urgency plus a door = thief. I can refuse without a debate.

Take the quiz. Module 2: fake surfaces — sites, apps, explorers, invoices, QR codes, and the pipes that deliver them.

lessons.title: Fake sites, ads, and lookalike domains
lessons.content:
# Fake sites, ads, and lookalike domains

**Phishing** is a surface that looks like a door you already trust. The transaction that empties you is honest. Your attention was not. The chain does not know that the logo was a costume. It only knows the signature was valid.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say why HTTPS is not honesty, why a search ad is not navigation, and how a calm-day bookmark is the tool you will actually have on a panic day.

## Where fakes sit, in 2026, for this academy’s students

They sit where you already look when you are hurried:

- **Sponsored ads** on search for “Trust Wallet”, “BscScan”, “PancakeSwap”, “Crystal Stones”, “the checkout processor”
- **Lookalike domains**: an extra letter, a hyphen, `crystalstones-claim.org`, `bscscan-fix.com`, `app-crystalstones.net`
- **Homograph domains**: Unicode letters that look like Latin. The address bar is lying to your eyes, not to the computer
- A reply under a real post, with the real logo, pointing at a new host
- A “mirror” someone pasted because the real site was “down for ten minutes”

**HTTPS** — the padlock — means the connection is encrypted *to that host*. The host may still be a thief. Thieves buy certificates. The padlock is not a character reference.

You already used a bookmark ritual for exchanges. Expand it until it is boring.

## The calm-day bookmark, used on the panic day

On a calm day, from a device you trust, type or navigate to:

- the academy site you actually use
- the official store page for the wallet app you actually use (Trust Wallet and MetaMask remain **examples**, not endorsements)
- BscScan, if that is your explorer for BNB Smart Chain
- the exchange you actually have an account on, if you have one
- the checkout processor only if you reached it from academy checkout, and only then save *that* checkout path
- PancakeSwap only if you actually use it — official domain saved, not a sponsored mirror

On panic day you do not search. You tap the bookmark. Search is an ad network with extra steps. Error messages are advertised against. “Crystal Stones official” as a query is a hunting ground.

If you do not have the bookmark yet, you are not “behind.” You are at the start of the ritual. Do it before Module 3. Do not do it from a link in this paragraph on a random mirror of the academy. You already know the site you enrolled on.

TABLE
Clue | What it actually means | What you do
Urgency + official logo | Default hostile | Bookmark, or nothing
New domain, old logo | Hostile | Do not connect
HTTPS padlock | Encrypted to *that* host | Still check the name
You arrived from an ad | Hostile until a bookmark exists | Close the tab
Extra word: claim, fix, migrate, support | Costume | Close the tab
Real site, banner “connect to unfreeze” | Often a malvertising slot | Ignore the banner; use the core page
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student googles “BscScan Crystal Stones” to add a token. They tap the first result. It is an ad. They connect a wallet and approve a spender named TokenFix. USDT leaves that night.

1. Real BscScan, opened later from a bookmark, even shows the approval. The book is not hiding.
2. The search ad was Door 4 opening Door 3. Nobody “broke cryptography.”
3. The contract they should have verified, if they were adding Crystal Stones at all, is `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` — a **verify** step, not a buy order, and not something an ad should introduce.
4. The fix going forward is not “I will read ads more carefully.” It is “I will not use search as a navigation tool for money.”

DIAGRAM
Calm day
  type known URL or use a source you already trust
  confirm the host name with your eyes
  save a bookmark
Panic day
  tap the bookmark
  do not search
  do not tap an ad
  do not "just this once"

Search ads are not a navigation tool.
ENDDIAGRAM

## If you already connected on a maybe-fake site

Assume Door 3 may be open even if you “only connected.” Connecting is not always an approval, but many clone sites queue a signature next, and people remember the connect, not the sign. Check approvals from a known tool later (Module 4). Do **not** go back to the fake site to “disconnect.” Disconnect on the fake site is theatre. It does not unload a spender on the chain.

If you typed a seed into that site, skip Module 4’s optimism. That is Door 1. Module 5: new wallet, clean device, test, move, retire. Do not ask the fake site to “release” you.

NOTE
This academy will not tell you that a particular colour of padlock, a particular badge, or a particular “verified” tick in a search result is safety. The ritual is slower and ruder: bookmark on a calm day, refuse novelty on a panic day. If that feels unsocial, good. Thieves are very social.
ENDNOTE

Homographs deserve one extra look: copy the host and paste it into a notes app in a large font. Your eye will sometimes catch a character the address bar rounded off. If anything looks even slightly off, you do not connect. There is no swap so urgent that a second look is expensive. The second look is the whole defence.

## What this lesson is for

So that “I googled it and the logo matched” stops being a sentence you say after a drain. Logos are cheap. Bookmarks are not glamorous. Bookmarks work.

## Say this out loud

- HTTPS is encryption to a host, not proof the host is honest.
- Ads are not navigation. Search is not a wallet address book.
- Bookmarks are for panic days. I save them on calm days.
- A fake site’s disconnect button does not close Door 3.
- If I typed a seed into a lookalike, I rotate. I do not negotiate with the lookalike.

Next: fake apps and APKs — the clone that does not need a website because it *is* the box you type the seed into.

lessons.title: Fake apps and APKs (sideloading Trust Wallet / MetaMask clones)
lessons.content:
# Fake apps and APKs (sideloading Trust Wallet / MetaMask clones)

A cloned wallet app does not need to break cryptography. It **is** the box you type the seed into. Door 1, with an icon you already trusted.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to refuse a store clone, refuse a chat APK, and say why a hardware wallet still fails if you confirm on a lying phone screen.

## Store clones

App stores are crowded. Similar name, similar icon, publisher you have never heard of, “Wallet Trust Pro”, “MetaMask Safe”, “Trust Wallet Official 2026.” Read the **publisher** name, not the title. Compare it, on a calm day, with the publisher you already used — or with the company site you bookmarked, not with a Telegram screenshot.

Install counts can be gamed. A 200-install “official” is a smell. A 10-million-install clone has also existed. Counts are a weak clue. Publisher identity plus a bookmark to the *store listing itself* is a stronger one. Save the listing, not the search query.

iOS has a cousin: enterprise profiles and “TestFlight from a helper.” A stranger’s profile on your phone is Door 1 wearing a lab coat. No.

## APK from chat

An **APK** is an Android package — an installer file. A Telegram or WhatsApp file named `Trust_Wallet_update.apk` is, for our purposes, malware. **Sideloading** means installing from that file instead of from the store. It skips even the already-weak store checks.

There is no BSC migration that arrives as a group file. There is no Crystal Stones academy update that arrives as an APK. There is no hardware-wallet companion that must be installed from a “tech admin.” Official updates: the store listing you already used, or the maker’s site you bookmarked.

If a phone is already a playground of random APKs — battery boosters, “WhatsApp plus,” movie loaders — **do not** generate a serious seed on it. The OS may already have overlay malware. An **overlay** draws a fake window on top of a real app when you copy an address or type a seed. You think you are in Trust Wallet. You are in a form.

Keep OS updates on. Delete junk. If you cannot, use a cleaner device for anything that is not play money.

TABLE
Source | Verdict | Why
Official store, correct publisher, listing you saved on a calm day | Default for a play pocket | Still not a halo, but it is the ordinary path
Store, similar name, new publisher | No | Costume
APK in WhatsApp / Telegram / “drive link” | No | Treat as malware
“TestFlight / enterprise profile” from a stranger | No | They own a gate on the phone
“Update required to keep BEP-20” as a file | No | There is no such update channel
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A student updates Trust Wallet from a pinned group APK because the caption said “BSC migration, old app will not send.” The app opens and asks for the seed “to resync.”

1. There is no such migration. Wallet apps can add networks without eating the seed.
2. The APK was a form. Everything that wallet ever held, and will receive, is now shared with the publisher of the file.
3. “I will just use it as a burner” is not a plan. The thief waits for the next deposit.
4. Honest next step: new seed on a *different*, cleaner device, official store listing, paper backup, test, move what remains if anything remains, retire the old words. Module 5. Not: ask the group admin who posted the APK to “help recover.”

DIAGRAM
Real app update
  store listing you already used
  publisher name you already checked
  no seed prompt on ordinary open

Fake update
  file in chat
  new publisher
  seed prompt on first open
  "migration" story

Hardware still fails if
  phone UI says 10 USDT to a friend
  device screen says a different 0x
  and you tap confirm anyway
ENDDIAGRAM

## Hardware does not bless a blind tap

A hardware wallet keeps the seed in a small computer that does not browse the web. Useful. Not magic. The laptop or phone still *proposes* the transaction. If the phone is compromised, it can propose a different destination than the one you think you see in the app.

You must read the **device screen** for destination and amount. If the phone shows 10 USDT to your friend and the device shows a different `0x`, you refuse. “Hardware wallet means I can sign anything blindly” is how expensive hardware becomes an expensive yes-machine.

Cheap clones of hardware devices exist. Buy from the maker, not a random marketplace listing with a seed card already filled in. A pre-filled seed is a wallet the seller already knows.

NOTE
This course will not name a “safe APK site.” There isn’t one for your purposes. If a device cannot use the official store, it is not a device for a savings seed. Play money on a junk phone is still play money — treat it as already shared.
ENDNOTE

If a family member already sideloaded the clone, treat their seed as leaked even if they “didn’t type it yet.” Overlay malware can catch the next paste. Rotation on a cleaner device is cheaper than a debate about whether the APK “looked official.” Official is a store listing you saved, not a feeling about an icon.

## What this lesson is for

So that “I updated from the group” stops sounding like IT hygiene. Groups are not app stores. Seed prompts on first open are not migrations. Hardware screens are the authority, not the colourful UI.

## Say this out loud

- A cloned app harvests the seed at the door. It does not need to hack the chain.
- An APK in chat is a no. Sideloading is not how Trust Wallet or MetaMask honestly update.
- Serious seeds are not born on junk phones full of random installers.
- If the hardware screen and the phone UI disagree, I refuse. The device screen wins.
- A pre-filled hardware seed card is the seller’s wallet.

Next: fake explorers, fake tickets, and fake the checkout processor pages — the costumes that sit on top of the “I always check BscScan” muscle.

lessons.title: Fake explorers, fake tickets, fake the checkout processor pages
lessons.content:
# Fake explorers, fake tickets, fake the checkout processor pages

You trained the muscle: “check BscScan.” Attackers trained too. They built **bscscan** with an extra letter. They built ticket portals that look like Binance (still **an example of a centralised exchange**). They built “Crystal Stones KYC” pages. They built the checkout processor invoices that expire in eleven minutes.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to use an explorer without connecting a wallet, refuse a ticket link that arrived as a reply, and refuse a payment page you did not open from academy checkout.

## Fake explorers

A fake explorer can show a transaction that never existed. It can show a real transaction and swap the token icon. It can show “failed — rebroadcast to finish” with a Connect Wallet button. Real BscScan does not need your keys to show a **public hash**. A hash is an id. Public data is public. “Connect to decode” is the tell.

Ad banners **on** real explorers have historically been dangerous. Ignore connect-to-unfreeze banners even on the real domain. The core pages still work without them. Your job is the address, the token contract, the method, the spender — not the carnival at the edge of the page.

Bookmark the explorer on a calm day. Paste the hash. Do not connect. If you need token-approval pages later, you will open them from *that same bookmarked host*, not from an ad that says “revoke now.”

## Fake tickets

You complain in public: “withdrawal stuck.” A link arrives: `secure-ticket.binance-support.help`. It wants login plus 2FA. That is Door 2, gift-wrapped as customer care.

Official support starts **inside** the bookmarked app or site. You open it. You create the ticket. You do not start from a reply-guy under your tweet, a WhatsApp number, or a “security desk” that DMed first. Display names are costumes. Blue ticks in one app are not a court in another.

## Fake the checkout processor and fake academy billing

Paid tracks in this academy, when they are live, checkout as **USDT on BEP-20 via the published academy checkout**. Not Crystal Stones token. Not PaynovaX. Not a personal wallet. The path starts on the **bookmarked academy site**.

A PDF invoice in email, a WhatsApp message with a QR, a “your certificate is on hold, pay 40 USDT,” a page that looks like the checkout processor but whose host is `nowpaynents.com` — those are phishing surfaces. If you did not click Checkout in the official app, you do not owe that invoice. There is no academy staff who will hurry you in a DM because a payment “will expire and your progress will reset.”

Fake Crystal Stones sites belong here too. A clone with a claim button, a “new contract,” or a mining dashboard that needs an approve to *view* is Door 3 in a crystal skin. The contract to verify remains `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. Verify on bookmarked BscScan. Do not verify on the clone’s own explorer widget.

TABLE
Real | Fake
Bookmarked BscScan, paste hash, no connect | Connect to view a public hash; “rebroadcast”; unfreeze banner
In-app exchange support you opened | Login portal from a reply-guy
Academy dashboard progress and platform certificates | Mint-your-cert dApp, WhatsApp the checkout processor invoice
Checkout you started in the bookmarked app | Invoice that arrived as a file, a QR, or a countdown
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Alex pastes a real hash into a fake explorer from a Google ad because the page said the real BscScan was “congested.” The fake page says the transaction failed and a button will “re-broadcast if you sign.” He signs a permit. USDT leaves.

1. The real BscScan, opened from his bookmark, already showed success. He paid a tax on not using the bookmark.
2. “Re-broadcast” is not a thing you owe a stranger. If a transaction is genuinely stuck, that is a nonce / gas story on a real wallet, later, calmly — not a signature on an ad.
3. He writes the drain hash in a notebook. He does not send it to a wizard who appeared under the same ad.
4. He checks approvals from the bookmarked explorer’s own tools, after he can breathe.

DIAGRAM
Need to check a hash
  --> bookmark explorer, paste hash, no connect

Need support
  --> you open the bookmarked app, you start the ticket

Need to pay this academy
  --> you start checkout in the bookmarked academy site
  --> USDT BEP-20 / the checkout processor when that is live

Never
  --> ad, connect, rebroadcast, unfreeze
  --> WhatsApp invoice, PDF, countdown
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
If a page needs your wallet to *show you* a public fact, it is not an explorer. If a page needs your seed to *show you* a ticket, it is not support. If a page needs a personal-wallet payment to *show you* a certificate, it is not this academy.
ENDNOTE

Fake the checkout processor pages often copy the logo and the countdown and change one letter in the host. If you did start checkout in the academy app, you still compare the host to what the app opened — not to a screenshot a “billing desk” sent after. A second invoice for the same course is a costume. One published checkout is enough.

## What this lesson is for

So the muscles you built — “check the explorer,” “open a ticket,” “pay tuition” — do not get stolen by costumes of themselves. Same jobs. Official doors only.

## Say this out loud

- Explorers do not need keys to show public data. Connect-to-view is a fake-explorer move.
- Ticket links in DMs are Door 2. I start support from a bookmark.
- Academy checkout is published, USDT BEP-20, not a WhatsApp the checkout processor QR.
- Banners that unfreeze or rebroadcast are drains, even on a real domain’s ad slot.
- A Crystal Stones clone with a new contract is a clone. I verify on bookmarked BscScan.

Next: QR codes, clipboard malware, and paste attacks — when your eyes read a sticker and your phone reads different bytes.

lessons.title: QR codes, clipboard malware, and paste attacks
lessons.content:
# QR codes, clipboard malware, and paste attacks

Your eyes read stickers, captions, and the first six characters of an `0x`. Your phone reads bytes. Attackers use the gap. This is Door 4 dressing a Door 1-adjacent failure: you still signed. You signed the wrong destination.

By the end of this lesson you should check a decoded address in text, check middle characters after a paste, and refuse to copy a lookalike from dust in your history.

## QR codes

A **QR code** is a picture of data. A poster, a “invoice,” a conference badge, a WhatsApp image, a the checkout processor lookalike. The caption can show the project’s known prefix. The QR can encode a different address.

**Read the decoded `0x` in your wallet before sending.** If the wallet cannot show the destination in text, do not send serious value. A test send is still allowed after you read the text — not instead of reading it.

Event QR is a favourite because you are standing up, someone is waiting, and pride does not want to be the person who decodes. Be that person. Merchants who are honest will wait for a test. Merchants who will not wait were not going to give you the goods anyway.

## Clipboard malware

You copy an address. Something on the device swaps it for a **vanity twin** — an address whose first and last characters look like yours or like your contact’s. You paste, glance at the ends, and send.

Defence: check **middle** characters, not only the prefix and suffix. Check on a second line of the UI. If you use hardware, the device screen is the authority. A second device’s wallet receive screen is a useful cross-check for savings-size sends.

If the clipboard keeps changing `0x` strings by itself, stop using that OS user account for funds. Treat the device as dirty. If you typed a seed on it, treat Door 1 as maybe-open. Rotate on a clean device. Do not “scan for viruses” via an APK a group drops. That is the same lesson as Module 2’s last one, wearing a helper hat.

## Address poisoning

**Address poisoning** is dust incoming from an address that looks like one you used before. Later you copy **that** lookalike from the transaction history, because history is easier than opening a contact. You send the real payment to the poisoner.

Defence: copy from contacts / bookmarked receive screens / a notebook you wrote on a calm day, not from a random incoming dust transaction. Hide junk tokens. Do not treat inbound dust as a convenient address book.

Paste attacks also include: a helper who pastes “their” address into your chat, then edits the message; a PDF invoice whose visible number does not match the copyable field; a group admin who posts an address, then a second account posts a “correction.” Copy once from a source you already trusted, then check middles, then test.

TABLE
Trick | What you think you sent | Defence
QR caption does not match payload | The caption’s address | Read decoded destination in the wallet, then test
Clipboard swap to a vanity twin | Your contact (ends match) | Middle digits + hardware or second device
Poison dust in history | An address you “used before” | Never copy from mystery inners; use contacts
Edited chat message | The first paste | Re-check middles at send time
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Maya pays a merchant QR at a campus event. The poster shows a Crystal Stones community prefix she recognises. Her wallet decodes a different address.

1. She does not send the rest of the week’s stall money.
2. She sends a test of play size. The test lands in an unknown wallet on bookmarked BscScan.
3. She does not send the rest. She does not argue with the stall about “the chain.” She leaves.
4. The test fee was tuition. Pride would have sent the rest. Pride is not a threat model.

DIAGRAM
Caption / sticker / chat text
        |
        |  (may lie)
        v
QR bytes or clipboard bytes
        |
        v
Wallet shows decoded destination as text
        |
        v
You read middles, not only ends
        |
        v
Test send  -->  bookmark explorer agrees  -->  then the rest, if ever
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
If clipboard malware is in the room, “I will paste more carefully” is not a full fix. A dirty OS plus a typed seed is a rotation event. Cleaning theatre (random APK scanners, “optimizer” apps) is how Door 1 gets a second form. New hot wallet on a clean device if the words may have been seen.
ENDNOTE

For savings-size sends, a second device showing the receive screen is not paranoia. It is how you notice a clipboard swap before the explorer does. Pride that refuses a test send at a stall is more expensive than the stall’s impatience. Honest merchants wait. Dishonest ones needed you hurried.

## What this lesson is for

So that your eyes stop being the only parser. Captions lie. Ends of addresses are a costume. Middles, decoded text, test sends, and hardware screens are the actual tools. If a stall will not wait for a test, you did not lose a customer relationship. You avoided a gift you would have called a payment.

## Say this out loud

- QR captions can lie. I read the decoded destination in the wallet.
- Clipboard malware is why middle characters matter, not only the first and last.
- Poison dust is bait for my copy-paste. I copy from contacts, not from mystery inners.
- If the clipboard rewrites addresses, I treat the device as dirty.
- A test send is cheaper than pride.

If a QR and a caption disagree, you already have the whole lesson. You do not need to diagnose malware. You need to not send the rest. The stall can wait. Your rent cannot come back from a wrong 0x.

Next: the panic-day procedure — a script you can run when a banner says you have ten minutes and your hands are already shaking.

lessons.title: The panic-day procedure (stop, disconnect, official bookmarks only)
lessons.content:
# The panic-day procedure (stop, disconnect, official bookmarks only)

When a screen says “your funds will be lost in 10 minutes,” that timer is a **prop**. Thieves need your cortisol. Chains do not confiscate for ignoring a banner. This academy does not run a confiscation clock. Exchanges do not unsuspend accounts because you typed an OTP into Telegram.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to run a short procedure from memory: stop, reject, bookmarks only, name the door, and not search the error into ads.

## The procedure

1. **Put the phone down.** You have time. Stand up if you can. Twenty minutes of nothing is cheaper than twenty seconds of a permit.
2. If a popup is open in a wallet, **Reject**. Reject is a complete sentence. You do not need to finish reading a hex blob to reject it.
3. Close the suspicious tab. Disconnect the wallet from *your wallet app’s* connected-sites list if you know how, on a bookmarked app — not on the fake site’s Disconnect button.
4. Open only **bookmarks** you saved on a calm day: academy, exchange, explorer, wallet vendor store listing. If you have no bookmark for this job, the answer is wait, not search.
5. **Name the door:** device, account, chain permission, human. Naming picks the next module’s fix. Guessing picks a helper DM.
6. If you already signed something, go to Module 5 (first hour) — not to a helper DM, not to a group with “I got hacked.” Impersonators are faster than friends.
7. Do not search the error message in Google and tap ads. Error messages are advertised against. “Nonce too high,” “execution reverted,” “approval expired” are hunting queries.

If you already typed a seed in the last ten minutes, this procedure is not enough. Skip to Module 5 rotation. Reject and bookmarks will not unsay words a form already collected. The phone down still helps — so you do not type them a second time into a “confirm.”

## What you will feel, named so it does not surprise you

Shame. Hurry. The need to tell a group so someone competent can take the wheel. Groups in that minute attract impersonators. If you must talk, talk to a human you already know **offline**, and still do not read them the seed, the OTP, or the backup codes.

Anger at yourself is a Door 4 opening. People sign the second thing because they want the first mistake to have been “not that bad.” It can wait. Remaining funds first. Story later.

TABLE
Urge | Replacement
Google the error + tap an ad | Bookmark docs, or wait
DM the admin who just appeared | No. Offline human if needed, still no seed
Send again to “unstick” | Explorer first, from a bookmark
Type seed into a reset / migration | Never
Pay a small unlock fee | Never
Install the APK the group dropped | Never
Share screen with a helper | Never
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** A banner: “Your USDT approval is expired. Renew in 8 minutes or lose the airdrop. Crystal Stones official.” The logo is correct-looking. The domain is not in her bookmarks.

1. She rejects the popup. She puts the phone down. She walks to the kitchen.
2. Later she opens bookmarked BscScan. There is no such approval. There is no such airdrop on the contract she already verified, if she holds it at all: `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`.
3. The airdrop was fake. The timer was a prop. Cortisol was the product.
4. She does not go back to the banner site to “disconnect.” She does not ask the fan group. She adds nothing to her bookmarks from that domain.

That is a successful panic day: nothing signed, nothing sent, nothing explained to strangers.

DIAGRAM
Banner timer
   |
   v
Reject popup --> phone down --> bookmarks only --> name the door
   |
   X ads
   X DMs
   X second send
   X seed reset
   X APK
   X screen share
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
There is no on-chain airdrop that requires a seed typed into a website. There is no academy timer that confiscates a wallet. There is no honest “verify by sending USDT.” Those three sentences are enough for most banners. If a real system needs you, it will still need you after you have opened a bookmark.
ENDNOTE

## Disconnect, said carefully

Disconnect means: stop talking to the hostile site. In the wallet app, remove the site from connected sites if the UI exists. On the chain, disconnect does **not** revoke an approval. People confuse the two because the words sound related. Module 4 is revoke. Today: do not return to the fake site to click its Disconnect as if that were a spell.

If you are not sure whether you signed, assume you might have. Check the explorer. Check approvals when you are calm. Do not check by reconnecting to the same host “to see.”

## What this lesson is for

So that hurry has a script. Scripts beat slogans. You will not become a calmer person in ten minutes. You can become a person with seven steps. If you freeze and cannot remember seven, remember three: reject, phone down, bookmarks only. The rest of the list will still be here when your hands work.

## Say this out loud

- Timers on banners are props. Chains do not confiscate for ignoring them.
- Reject, phone down, bookmarks only, name the door.
- I do not search errors into ads. I do not finish a process in a DM.
- Shame is not a reason to open Door 1.
- Fake-site Disconnect does not unload a spender. Revoke is a different job, later, from a bookmark.

If you remember only one panic-day picture, make it this: the timer is theatre, the bookmark is the door, the group is a hunting ground. Twenty minutes of nothing is a successful defence.

Next: email, SMS, WhatsApp, and Telegram — the pipes that deliver every fake surface in this module.

lessons.title: Email, SMS, WhatsApp, and Telegram as delivery pipes
lessons.content:
# Email, SMS, WhatsApp, and Telegram as delivery pipes

The fake site, the fake APK, the fake invoice, the panic banner — they have to *arrive*. They arrive through pipes you already live in: email, SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, sometimes X. The pipe is not the thief. The pipe is how the costume gets a face.

By the end of this lesson you should treat unsolicited money-messages as hostile by default, know what each pipe is good at stealing, and refuse the sentence “but it came from the academy group.”

## Email

Email is Door 2’s favourite hallway. Password resets, “Your Binance login from a new device,” “the checkout processor invoice attached,” “Crystal Stones certificate PDF.” The logo will match. The host in the button will not.

Rules that survive tired eyes:

- Open exchanges and the academy from bookmarks, not from buttons in mail.
- A reset you did not ask for is a signal to lock the account from a bookmark — not a reason to click the email’s button.
- Attachments that want macros, APKs, or “view invoice online” are Door 1 or Door 4. Delete.
- Password reuse is how a leaked shopping site becomes an exchange session. Unique passwords. A password manager is boring and adult.

## SMS

SMS is weak 2FA and a strong panic channel. “Your USDT will be frozen, visit …” is not a bank and not an exchange. **SIM-swap** is when someone moves your number to a SIM they hold, then intercepts OTPs. Defence: do not use SMS as the only 2FA on an exchange if the product offers an authenticator app. Keep the mobile operator’s real shop number written on paper. If swap is in progress, you call *that* number, not a number a text just sent.

SMS that names Crystal Stones, BscScan, or the checkout processor is not from us. We do not collect your phone number in this course to text you invoices.

## WhatsApp

WhatsApp is the local and many-country default for “someone I might know.” Display names are costumes. Forwarded status images are costumes. Voice notes can be cloned badly and still work on a hurried listener.

Typical payloads: fake jobs, fake mentors, P2P “I have paid, here is the receipt,” the checkout processor QRs, APKs, “your cousin’s new number,” a listing team. Official contact with this academy does not start as a cold WhatsApp. If a family member’s number asks for a seed, call them on a number you already had — voice, not the chat that just arrived.

P2P belongs here because it is a pipe problem as much as an exchange problem: a receipt is a picture. Pictures are not settlement. Settlement is the exchange’s own paid-status, or the chain’s own explorer, from a bookmark.

## Telegram (and “the academy group”)

Telegram is where fan groups, fake admins, airdrop bots, and recovery specialists live in a pile. A **verified** mark inside Telegram is not a court. Anyone can be “Crystal Stones Admin” in a group you do not control.

This academy’s classroom is the LMS you enrolled on. A public Telegram room — even a useful one — is not staff, not Mentor, not support, not a listing desk. Admins in fan groups cannot unsuspend a wallet. Bots that ask you to “verify” are Door 1 or Door 3. Mute, leave, bookmark the real site.

If you run a group, you are a target for hijack (loot type: audience). Guard admin rights. Never let a stranger “help moderate” with full rights. Never post a seed “as an example.”

TABLE
Pipe | What it is good at | Adult default
Email | Fake resets, fake invoices, malware attachments | Bookmark, don’t click; unique passwords
SMS | Panic links, OTP theft via SIM-swap | Authenticator over SMS; operator number on paper
WhatsApp | Costume of family, P2P receipts, APKs, mentor DMs | Call known numbers; receipts are not settlement
Telegram | Fake admins, bots, airdrops, recovery theatre | Fan groups are not staff; verify-bots are no
ENDTABLE

**Worked scenario.** Riley’s phone gets three messages in an hour: an SMS “BNB Smart Chain freeze, click to appeal”; a WhatsApp “Crystal Mentor” with a the checkout processor QR; a Telegram bot in a fan group, “verify wallet to keep CST airdrop.”

1. She names them as pipes, not as institutions. None of the three is the chain, the academy, or an exchange.
2. She does not click. She opens bookmarked academy, bookmarked exchange, bookmarked explorer. Nothing is frozen. Nothing is owed.
3. The WhatsApp QR is a personal address. “Verify by sending USDT” is on the never-list.
4. She does not warn the Telegram group with her remaining wallet address in the post. She may warn with the *domain* and the *bot name*. Remaining funds are not a public trophy.

DIAGRAM
Pipes:  email, SMS, WhatsApp, Telegram, ads, X replies
   |
   v
Costume arrives (logo, timer, invoice, APK, bot)
   |
   v
You start from a bookmark, or you do nothing
   |
   X You start from the pipe
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Being friendly on WhatsApp is allowed. Being available for seed-collection is not. You can reply “I will only continue inside the academy site I bookmarked” and then actually go there. If they cannot follow, they were never staff. Silence is also a complete answer.
ENDNOTE

X (Twitter) replies belong in the same family as Telegram: a logo under a pain post is a job. Mute, bookmark, official ticket. Do not argue the badge. Badges are cheaper than USDT. If you run a public account, say once in the bio that you will never DM a seed request or a recovery — then still assume clones will ignore the bio. The bio is for your actual audience, not for the costume.

## What this lesson is for

So that the delivery channel stops borrowing trust from the rest of your life. Family-shaped WhatsApp, bank-shaped SMS, academy-shaped Telegram — same refuse-line. Bookmark or nothing.

## Say this out loud

- Pipes deliver costumes. They do not become the academy, the exchange, or the chain.
- I do not click resets, invoices, or freeze appeals from mail or SMS. I open a bookmark.
- SMS 2FA can die in a SIM-swap. Authenticator plus paper backup codes is the adult pair.
- WhatsApp receipts are pictures. Fan-group admins are not staff. Verify-bots are a no.
- I can refuse in one sentence, or I can be silent. I do not need to win the chat.

Take the quiz. Module 3: people scams — giveaways, impersonation, jobs, romance, recovery specialists, and the last train.
